notable_claims: ISU implemented a policy blocking specific alt.* newsgroups from public machines.
Access to censored groups requires system administrators of department-owned machines to fill out a form.
classification.summary: A student at Iowa State University reports a new policy censoring specific Usenet newsgroups, primarily those related to sex and drugs, from public campus machines. Access to these groups is restricted to department-owned machines where administrators must submit a formal request for a full feed. The author seeks legal resources from the EFF to challenge this censorship.
classification.title: New news censorship policy at Iowa State University

identity.subject: New news censorship policy at Iowa State University

notable_claims: The university's restriction of newsgroups is described as blatant censorship.
The author claims that the U.S. Postal Service is not held liable for obscene materials sent by users, suggesting a similar legal standard should apply to network providers.
classification.summary: Mark D. Smucker protests a new Usenet policy at Iowa State University that bans specific newsgroups, characterizing the move as blatant censorship. He argues that university computing centers should follow library standards regarding access to controversial materials and asserts that legal responsibility for content lies with the authors, not the service provider.
classification.title: Re: New Usenet Policy on 1/6/92 - Standard List Definition

identity.subject: Re: New Usenet Policy on 1/6/92 - Standard List Definition

notable_claims: ISU's Usenet policy restricted access to alt.sex and alt.drugs for the general student body.
The university required users to sign a form to gain access to restricted newsgroups.
Restricting access based on machine type created an inequity between those with private machines and those using public terminals.
classification.summary: Michael L. Begley protests a new Usenet policy at Iowa State University (ISU) that restricted access to certain newsgroups, specifically alt.sex and alt.drugs. He argues that requiring students to sign a form for full access is an invasion of privacy and constitutes censorship. The post advocates for universal access by default, suggesting that users should opt-out rather than be forced to opt-in.
classification.title: The new netnews policy

notable_claims: The Computing Center lacked the technical ability to implement account-specific restrictions on Usenet news.
The primary motivation for the new policy was to transfer legal or administrative responsibility from the provider to the reader.
classification.summary: Shivanand Shenoy discusses a new Usenet policy at Iowa State University, noting that the Computing Center lacks the technology to implement account-specific restrictions. He explains that the policy's intent is to shift responsibility from the service provider to the individual reader. He suggests using Wylbur as an alternative to avoid perceived infringements of rights.
classification.title: Re: New Usenet News Policy on 1/6/92

identity.subject: Re: New Usenet News Policy on 1/6/92

notable_claims: The new newsgroup censorship policy was not approved by the Comp Ctr Newsgroup committee.
The University Computation Advisory Committee did not approve the policy.
classification.summary: John Hascall urges the community to protest a new newsgroup censorship policy at Iowa State University. He claims that both the Computation Center Newsgroup committee and the University Computation Advisory Committee rejected the policy before its implementation.

notable_claims: Adult-oriented newsgroups accounted for approximately 6.83% of total Usenet traffic in November 1991.
The alt.sex group had roughly 210,000 readers, representing 12.7% of all newsreaders at the time.
classification.summary: Lars P. Fischer responds to a claim that Usenet is primarily used for pornography, citing an article in the German version of EMMA. He provides statistical data on reader percentages and traffic volume to argue that while adult content exists, it does not constitute the majority of network usage.
classification.title: Re: The USENET pornographic network

classification.summary: Christa Keil discusses the censorship of Usenet newsgroups at universities. She criticizes the University of Stuttgart for blocking both sex-related groups and sci.military, arguing that such restrictions are based on misconceptions about the content.

notable_claims: Gaming in university labs is manageable through mutual respect and priority-based access.
Administrative tolerance of non-academic use reduces rebellious behavior among students.
classification.summary: Jason Steiner, a computer consultant at the University of Toledo, discusses the coexistence of gaming and academic work in university labs. He argues that mutual respect between administrators and students prevents conflict over resource usage. He suggests that tolerance from administration leads to better compliance from users when resources are needed for academic priorities.
classification.title: Re: Gaming

notable_claims: MUD traffic accounted for approximately 30% of total network usage during weekend/off-peak periods.
Campus policy prohibited MUD playing between 8am and midnight on school days.
Interactive response times for real-time MUD battles were insufficient on 56KB connections.
classification.summary: Brick Verser provides network traffic statistics from K-State to analyze the impact of Multi-User Dungeon (MUD) gaming on campus bandwidth. The data shows that despite policies prohibiting MUD play during school hours, it remained a top application by volume. The author notes that while T1 connections handle this traffic easily, 56KB connections suffered from latency issues affecting gameplay.
classification.title: Network utilization by MUD players

identity.subject: Network utilization by MUD players (was Re: Gaming)

notable_claims: Suggests charging users for terminal time to resolve conflicts between academic work and recreational gaming.
classification.summary: A discussion regarding the ethics and policy of gaming in university computer labs. The author responds to arguments about absolute freedom by suggesting a market-based solution where users pay for access time to manage scarce computing resources.
classification.title: Re: Gaming

notable_claims: Revelation of any information without the originator's permission is a violation of privacy.
Assumptions about what constitutes 'basic' public information are subjective and vary by individual.
classification.summary: John G. Otto argues against the involuntary disclosure of user information via network services like Finger. He contends that any revelation of personal data without the owner's explicit permission is a violation of privacy, regardless of whether the information is considered 'basic'.
classification.title: Re: Finger & Liberty
